newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish C/A gap fuelled by investment imports.
newsitem.headline: Polish C/A gap fuelled by investment imports.

text.p: Poland's trade gap jumped to $7.2 billion after 11 months of 1996 and might exceed eight billion in the whole of 1996 but prevailing imports are of a healthy, investment nature, analysts said on Wednesday.
The National Bank of Poland said the current account gap in the January-November period rose $125 million to $984 million against a $4,959 billion surplus in the same period of 1995.

"For an economy which is likely to have grown five to six percent in 1996 this is really a small current deficit...given that the structure of imports is very healthy," said Krzysztof Bledowski, chief economist at WoodCommerz in Warsaw.
According to the Centre for Strategic Studies (CSS), the former planning ministry, some 80 percent of Poland's imports are investment and 20 percent consumer goods.
"The imports are mostly investment, which is good and natural for a developing economy such as Poland," said Tadeusz Chroscicki, chief analyst at CSS.

"However, the rates of import and export growth are worrying, because they are too wide apart, and if that trend continues we might end up with a trade deficit of more than $11 billion in 1997," he said.
Exports in January-November against the period last year rose only 5.2 percent in dollar terms while imports in the same period rose 31.3 percent against the same period of 1995.
Analysts also noted the smaller inflows from cross-border trade which according to the NBP brought $6.7 billion in 11 months of 1996 against $7.1 billion in the same period of 1995.

"The easing of the 'grey zone' cross-border trade was to be expected as Poland comes closer and closer to the European Union in economic terms," said Krzysztof Rybinski, chief economist at ING bank in Warsaw.
Analysts said the worsening trade balance, although not a serious threat to the economy, could drain the country's currency reserves and exert a downward presure on the zloty.

"The trade gap and potential reserve fall will put a depreciation pressure on the zloty, but I doubt if the central bank will allow it to fall too much as it has said it wanted a stable currency," said Pawel Krawczykiewicz, analyst at PBI SA.
Official currency reserves rose $146 million in November to $17.85 billion and were $3.62 billion higher than a year ago.
Some analysts expected negative current account could deplete the reserves this year, but others said the zloty should be stable.
"Official reserves may fall by up to $2 billion, which does not jeopardise Poland's ability to pay off its foreign debt," said WoodCommerz's Bledowski.
"I would expect the trade gap in 1997 at $3-5 billion which does not call for changes in the zloty exchange rate mechanism or a zloty devaluation," he said.
Analysts also expected high investment imports to pay-off in the longer term, making Polish exports more competitive.

"The 1995 and 1996 investment boom will boost exports in the years to come bringing more equilibrium into trade, although Poland is likely to be stuck with a negative trade balance for many years," said CSS's Chroscicki.
